{{Short description|Fallacious approach to mislead an audience}}
{{About|the idiom and the logical fallacy|the type of preserved food|Kipper|other uses}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2023}}

[[File:A Study in Scarlet Friston 01.jpg|thumb|upright|In the mystery novel ''[[A Study in Scarlet]]'', the detective [[Sherlock Holmes]] examines a clue which is later revealed to be intentionally misleading.]]

A '''red herring''' is something that misleads or distracts from an important question, a relevant argument, or the solving of a mystery or crime.<ref name="oed">{{cite web |title=red herring, n. |url=http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/160314 |website=[[Oxford English Dictionary]] |publisher=OED Third Edition, September 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924085502/http://www.oed.com/view/Entry/160314 |archive-date=September 24, 2015}}</ref> It may be either a logical [[fallacy]] or a [[literary device]] that leads readers or audiences toward a false conclusion. A red herring may be used intentionally, as in [[mystery fiction]] or as part of [[rhetorical strategies]] (e.g., in [[politics]]), or may be used in argumentation inadvertently.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Red-Herring|date=15 May 2019|title=Red Herring|url=https://www.txstate.edu/philosophy/resources/fallacy-definitions/Red-Herring.html|access-date=31 August 2021|website=txstate.edu|language=en}}</ref>

The expression was popularized in 1807 by the English [[polemic]]ist [[William Cobbett]], who told a story of having used a [[kipper|strong-smelling smoked herring]] to divert and distract hounds from chasing a rabbit.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Dupriez|first=Bernard Marie|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uff2N62Jx9wC|title=A Dictionary of Literary Devices: Gradus, A–Z|year=1991|publisher=University of Toronto Press|isbn=978-0-8020-6803-3|language=en}}</ref>

== Logical fallacy ==
As an [[informal fallacy]], the red herring falls into a broad class of [[relevance]] fallacies. Unlike the [[straw man]], which involves a distortion of the other party's position,<ref name="Hurley2011">{{cite book|author=Hurley, Patrick J.|title=A Concise Introduction to Logic|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ikp2dGWT5O4C&pg=PT155|year=2011|publisher=Cengage Learning|isbn=978-0-8400-3417-5|pages=131–133|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222174516/https://books.google.com/books?id=Ikp2dGWT5O4C&pg=PT155|archive-date=22 February 2017}}</ref> the red herring is a seemingly plausible, though ultimately irrelevant, diversionary tactic.<ref name="Tindale2007">{{cite book|author=Tindale, Christopher W.|title=Fallacies and Argument Appraisal|url=https://archive.org/details/fallaciesargumen00tind|url-access=limited|year=2007|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-84208-2|pages=[https://archive.org/details/fallaciesargumen00tind/page/n47 28]–33}}</ref> According to the ''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]'', a red herring may be intentional or unintentional; it is not necessarily a conscious intent to mislead.<ref name="oed" />

The expression is mainly used to assert that an argument is not relevant to the issue being discussed. For example, "I think we should make the academic requirements stricter for students. I recommend you support this because we are in a budget crisis, and we do not want our salaries affected." The second sentence, though used to support the first sentence, does not address that topic.

== Intentional device ==
In fiction and non-fiction, a red herring may be a false clue intended to lead readers or audiences toward a mistaken conclusion.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RUXdoqa4wBAC&pg=PA142 |page=142 |author=Niazi, Nozar |title=How To Study Literature: Stylistic And Pragmatic Approaches |publisher=PHI Learning Pvt. Ltd. |year=2010 |access-date=2 March 2013 |isbn=978-81-203-4061-9 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131009041201/http://books.google.com/books?id=RUXdoqa4wBAC&pg=PA142 |archive-date=9 October 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/dictionaryoflite0000dupr |url-access=registration |title=Dictionary of Literary Devices: Gradus, A-Z |author=Dupriez, Bernard Marie |others=Translated by Albert W. Halsall |page=[https://archive.org/details/dictionaryoflite0000dupr/page/322 322] |publisher=University of Toronto Press |year=1991 |access-date=2 March 2013 |isbn=978-0-8020-6803-3 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=noTRMjASamEC&pg=PA143 |title=The Book of Literary Terms: The Genres of Fiction, Drama, Nonfiction, Literary Criticism and Scholarship |author=Turco, Lewis |page=143 |publisher=UPNE |year=1999 |access-date=2 March 2013 |isbn=978-0-87451-955-6 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131009041159/http://books.google.com/books?id=noTRMjASamEC&pg=PA143 |archive-date=9 October 2013 }}</ref> For example, the character of Bishop Aringarosa in [[Dan Brown]]'s ''[[The Da Vinci Code]]'' is presented for most of the novel as if he is at the centre of the church's conspiracies, but is later revealed to have been innocently duped by the true [[antagonist]] of the story. The character's name is a loose Italian translation of "red herring" ({{lang|it|aringa rosa}}; {{lang|it|rosa}} actually meaning {{gloss|pink}}, and very close to {{lang|it|rossa}}, {{gloss|red}}).<ref>{{cite book | title=The Oxford Handbook of the Reception History of the Bible | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iePi5FO-bxAC&pg=PA370 | page=370 | publisher=Oxford University Press | year=2011 | isbn=978-0-19-967039-0 |author1=Lieb, Michael |author2=Mason, Emma |author3=Roberts, Jonathan | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170222231515/https://books.google.com/books?id=iePi5FO-bxAC&pg=PA370 | archive-date=22 February 2017 }}</ref>

There is a red herring in the first [[Sherlock Holmes]] story, ''[[A Study in Scarlet]]'', where the murderer writes at the crime scene the word {{lang|de|Rache}} ('revenge' in German), leading the police{{mdash}}and the reader{{mdash}}to mistakenly presume that a German was involved.

A red herring is often used in legal studies and exam problems to mislead and distract students from reaching a correct conclusion about a legal issue, intended as a device that tests students' comprehension of underlying law and their ability to properly discern material factual circumstances.<ref>{{cite book|editor-last=Sheppard|editor-first=Steve |title=The history of legal education in the United States: commentaries and primary sources|date=2005|publisher=Lawbook Exchange|location=Clark, N.J.|isbn=978-1-58477-690-1|edition=2nd print.}}</ref>

== History ==
[[File:Red herring.jpg|thumb|[[Herring]]s "[[kipper]]ed" by smoking, salting and artificially dyeing until made reddish-brown, i.e., a "red herring". Prior to the existence of refrigeration, kipper was known for being strongly [[pungency|pungent]]. In 1807, William Cobbett claimed that he as a child together with other children used a kipper to lead [[hunting dog]]s away from the scent of a hare the children intended to hunt—an [[apocrypha]]l story that was probably the origin of the idiom.]]

{{quote box|author=—[[William Cobbett]], February 14, 1807|title=Continental War|source=''Cobbett's Political Register, Volume XI''<ref name="cobbett" />|quote=When I was a boy, we used [to], in order to draw off the [[Harrier (dog)|harriers]] from the trail of a [[hare]] that we had set down as our own private property, get to her haunt<ref>According to the [https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/haunt Collins English Dictionary], one meaning of ''haunt'' is a place at which one is regularly found, a hangout, and another meaning is a lair or feeding place of animals.</ref> early in the morning, and drag a red-herring, tied to a string, four or five miles over hedges and ditches, across fields and through coppices,{{efn|A ''coppice'', US English ''copse'', is a small group of trees growing very close to each other either naturally or due to being regularly trimmed back to stumps.}} till we got to a point, whence we were pretty sure the hunters would not return to the spot where they had [been] thrown off; and, though I would, by no means, be understood, as comparing the editors and proprietors of the London daily press to animals half so sagacious and so faithful as hounds, I cannot help thinking, that, in the case to which we are referring, they must have been misled, at first, by some political deceiver.|width=30%|border=4px|align=right}}

There is no fish species called "red herring." Rather, it is a name given to a particularly strong [[kipper]], made from fish (typically [[herring]]) strongly [[Curing (food preservation)|cured]] in [[brine]] or heavily [[Smoking (cooking)|smoked]]. This process makes the fish particularly pungent-smelling and, with strong enough brine, turns its flesh reddish.<ref name="quinion2002">{{cite web | author=Quinion, Michael | year=2002–2008 | title=The Lure of the Red Herring | work=[[World Wide Words]] | url=http://www.worldwidewords.org/articles/herring.htm | access-date=10 November 2010 | author-link=Michael Quinion | url-status=live | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101104180714/http://www.worldwidewords.org/articles/herring.htm | archive-date=4 November 2010 }}</ref> In this literal sense, as a strongly cured kipper, the term can be dated to the late 13th century in the Anglo-Norman poem ''[[The Treatise (Walter of Bibbesworth)|The Treatise]]'' by [[Walter of Bibbesworth]], which then first appears in Middle English in the early 14th century: "{{lang|enm|He eteþ no ffyssh / But heryng red.|italic=no}}"<ref name="oed" /> A 15th-century text known as the Heege Manuscript includes a joke about fighting oxen chopping one another apart until only "three red herrings" remain.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Almeroth-Williams |first1=Tom |title='Bawdy bard' manuscript reveals medieval roots of British comedy |url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/bawdy-bard-act-discovered-revealing-fifteenth-century-roots-of-british-comedy |access-date=8 February 2024 |work=University of Cambridge |date=31 May 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

The [[figurative sense]] of "red herring" has traditionally been said to originate from a supposed technique of training [[scent hound]]s.<ref name="quinion2002" /> There are variations of the story, but according to one version, the pungent red herring would be dragged along a trail until a puppy learned to follow the scent.<ref>[[Thomas Nashe|Nashe, Thomas]]. (1599) [http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf ''Nashes Lenten Stuffe''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715030947/http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf |date=15 July 2011 }} "Next, to draw on hounds to a sent, to a redde herring skinne there is nothing comparable." (Since Nashe makes this statement not in a serious reference to hunting but as an aside in a humorous pamphlet, the professed aim of which is to extol the wonderful virtues of red herrings, it need not be evidence of actual practice. In the same paragraph he makes other unlikely claims, such as that the fish dried and powdered is a prophylactic for kidney or gallstones.)</ref> Later, when the dog was being trained to follow the faint odour of a [[Fox hunting|fox]] or a [[badger]], the trainer would drag a red herring perpendicular to the animal's trail to confuse the dog.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.jal.2008.09.004 |first1=J.E.P |last1=Currall  |year=2008 |title=Authenticity: a red herring? |journal=Journal of Applied Logic |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=534–544 |issn=1570-8683|last2=Moss |first2=M.S. |last3=Stuart |first3=S.A.J. |url=http://eprints.gla.ac.uk/4658/1/4658.pdf }}</ref> The dog eventually learned to follow the original scent rather than the stronger scent. A variation of this story is given, without mention of its use in training, in ''The Macmillan Book of Proverbs, Maxims, and Famous Phrases'' (1976), with the earliest use cited being from W. F. Butler's ''Life of Napier'', published in 1849.<ref>[[Burton Stevenson|Stevenson, Burton]] (ed.) (1976) [1948] ''The Macmillan Book of Proverbs, Maxims, and Famous Phrases'' New York: Macmillan. p. 1139. {{ISBN|978-0-02-614500-8}}</ref> ''[[Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable]]'' (1981) gives the full phrase as "Drawing a red herring across the path", an idiom meaning "to divert attention from the main question by some side issue"; here, once again, a "dried, smoked and salted" herring when "drawn across a fox's path destroys the scent and sets the hounds at fault."<ref>Evans, Ivor H. (ed.) (1981) ''[[Brewer's Dictionary of Phrase and Fable]]'' (Centenary edition, revised) New York: Harper & Row. p.549. {{ISBN|978-0-06-014903-1}}</ref> Another variation of the dog story is given by Robert Hendrickson (1994) who says escaping convicts used the pungent fish to throw off hounds in pursuit.<ref>Hendrickson, Robert (2000). ''The Facts on File Encyclopedia of Word and Phrase Origins''. United States: Checkmark.</ref>

According to a pair of articles by Professor Gerald Cohen and Robert Scott Ross published in ''Comments on Etymology'' (2008), supported by etymologist [[Michael Quinion]] and accepted by the ''[[Oxford English Dictionary]]'', the idiom did not originate from a hunting practice.<ref name="quinion2002" /> Ross researched the origin of the story and found the earliest reference to using herrings for training animals was in a tract on horsemanship published in 1697 by Gerland Langbaine.<ref name="quinion2002" /> Langbaine recommended a method of training horses (not hounds) by dragging the carcass of a cat or fox so that the horse would be accustomed to following the chaos of a hunting party.<ref name="quinion2002" /> He says if a dead animal is not available, a red herring would do as a substitute.<ref name="quinion2002" /> This recommendation was misunderstood by Nicholas Cox, published in the notes of another book around the same time, who said it should be used to train hounds (not horses).<ref name="quinion2002" /> Either way, the herring was not used to distract the hounds or horses from a trail, rather to guide them along it.<ref name="quinion2002" />

A slightly different metaphorical usage of "red herring" appears in a 1682 pamphlet printed by [[Richard Baldwin (publisher)| Richard Baldwin]], defending the [[Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury|Earl of Shaftesbury]]: "But your Lordships business is, to keep your Hounds in full cry, against the pretended Association, for since you cannot find one really in being; a red-herring from your own Kitchen, must be hunted and trail'd through the Kingdom, to make a noise."<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A51081.0001.001?rgn=main;view=fulltext|title=A modest account of the present posture of affairs in England with particular reference to the Earl of Shaftsbury's case, and a vindication of him from two pretended letters of a noble peer / by a person of quality|date=1682|page=2}}</ref>

The earliest reference to using herring for distracting hounds is an article published on 14 February 1807 by the radical journalist [[William Cobbett]] in his [[polemic]]al periodical ''[[Political Register]]''.<ref name="quinion2002" /><ref name="oed" /><ref name="cobbett">{{Cite book|last=Cobbett|first=William|url=http://archive.org/details/cobbettspolitica11cobb|title=Cobbett's Political Register|date=1807|volume=11|place=London|publisher=Bagshaw|at=col. 232|quote="...we used [to], in order to draw off the harriers from the trail of a hare that we had set down as our own private property, get to her haunt early in the morning, and drag a red-herring, tied to a string, four or five miles over hedges and ditches..."}}</ref>{{efn|For the full original story by Cobbett, see the "Continental War" section in {{cite book |last1=Cobbett |first1=William |title=Cobbett's political register |date=1807|publisher=Richard Bagshaw |location=London |pages=231–234 |url=https://archive.org/details/cobbettspolitica11cobb/page/116/mode/2up }}}}

According to Cohen and Ross, and as accepted by the OED, this is the origin of the figurative meaning of red herring.<ref name="quinion2002" /> In the piece, William Cobbett critiques the English press, which had mistakenly reported Napoleon's defeat. Cobbett recounted that he had once used a red herring to deflect hounds in pursuit of a hare, adding "It was a mere transitory effect of the political red-herring; for, on the Saturday, the scent became as cold as a stone."<ref name="quinion2002" /> Quinion concludes: "This story, and [Cobbett's] extended repetition of it in 1833, was enough to get the figurative sense of ''red herring'' into the minds of his readers, unfortunately also with the false idea that it came from some real practice of huntsmen."<ref name="quinion2002" />

Although Cobbett popularized the figurative usage, he was not the first to consider red herring for scenting hounds in a literal sense; an earlier reference occurs in the pamphlet ''Nashe's Lenten Stuffe'', published in 1599 by the Elizabethan writer [[Thomas Nashe]], in which he says "Next, to draw on hounds to a scent, to a red herring skin there is nothing comparable."<ref name="Nashe">[[Thomas Nashe|Nashe, Thomas]] (1599) [http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf ''Praise of the Red Herring''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715030947/http://www.oxford-shakespeare.com/Nashe/Nashes_Lenten_Stuff.pdf |date=15 July 2011 }} In: William Oldys and John Malham (Eds) [https://books.google.com/books?id=JxOjdlsWMGcC&dq=%22on+hounds+to+a+scent%22&pg=PA331 ''The Harleian miscellany''] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171230213316/https://books.google.co.nz/books?id=JxOjdlsWMGcC&pg=PA331&lpg=PA331&dq=%22on+hounds+to+a+scent%22&source=bl&ots=LZlI9hToJr&sig=aqRgPgjXnFakagAqVgvlw9YpOtY&hl=en&sa=X&ei=3JUuT4rlGOa5iQfnoNjdDg&ved=0CCEQ6AEwAA |date=30 December 2017 }} Volume 2, Printed for R. Dutton, 1809. p. 331.</ref> The ''Oxford English Dictionary'' makes no connection with Nashe's quote and the figurative meaning of red herring to distract from the intended target, only in the literal sense of a hunting practice to draw dogs toward a scent.<ref name="oed" />

The use of herring to distract pursuing scent hounds was tested on [[MythBusters (2010 season)#Episode 148 – Hair of the Dog|Episode 148]] of the series ''[[MythBusters]]''.<ref>{{IMDb title|qid=Q130342815|id=tt1683693|title=MythBusters: Season 9, Episode 1 – Hair of the Dog}}</ref> Although the hound used in the test stopped to eat the fish and lost the fugitive's scent temporarily, it eventually backtracked and located the target, resulting in the idea's being classified by the show as a "Busted" myth.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Episode 148: Hair of the Dog|url=http://mythbustersresults.com/hair-of-the-dog|url-status=usurped|website=MythBusters Results|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211231130225/http://mythbustersresults.com/hair-of-the-dog/ |archive-date=31 December 2021|access-date=25 January 2023}}</ref>
